sourceGap.natural: the 'she' Korean built for print in the early twentieth century — read on every page of every novel, said aloud by nobody
sourceGap.note: This module's 그녀 is younger than the grandmothers who read it: Korean had no separate 'she' until novelists of the 1920s, translating and imitating Japanese fiction, copied 彼女 (that-woman) character for character — M29's 그 + the 女 of M4's 여자 — to give their heroines a pronoun. Before that, prose used 그 for anyone, and it still does for men; 그녀 is the only gendered pronoun the language owns, and it never crossed into the mouth. Say 그녀 in conversation and you sound like a subtitle; the mouth points (그 사람, M55's 걔) or names (M4's 씨). The complaint that it is a Japanese import and should be retired surfaces every decade, and every decade the novels keep it. A word that shows what the written register is: not older Korean, but a Korean built for the page.
